worksheet.title: Build Bit's Stack
worksheet.subtitle: Draw the blocks to get Bit to the star
worksheet.learning_goal: I can build a short program to get Bit to the star.

parts.title: You build it
parts.text: Now YOU make the program. Draw an arrow in each empty block so Bit reaches the star ★. Use ➡ to go right and ⬅ to go left. Then run your stack from the top to check Bit lands on the star.

parts.title: Build 1 — Bit on box 1, star on box 4
Get to the star
parts.prompt: Draw an arrow in each of the 3 empty blocks so Bit goes from box 1 to the star on box 4. Then run it to check.

parts.title: Build 2 — Bit on box 4, star on box 2
Your program
parts.note: The star is to the LEFT this time.

parts.title: Go left to the star
parts.prompt: Draw an arrow in each of the 2 empty blocks so Bit goes from box 4 to the star on box 2. Then run it to check.

parts.title: Build 3 — Bit on box 1, star on box 3
You try — build it yourself
parts.prompt: Draw an arrow in each of the 2 empty blocks so Bit goes from box 1 to the star on box 3. Then run it to check.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: You wrote a program! You picked the blocks and put them in order to make Bit reach the goal. That is what coders do — then they run it to make sure it works.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Kindergarten · Intro Block Coding
teacher_guide.title: Build Bit's Stack
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children build their own stack — choosing and ordering move blocks — to make Bit reach the star, then run it to check. Turning a goal ("get to box 4") into an ordered set of blocks is the writing side of coding. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper, a pencil, and a crayon. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: paper blocks (a green flag block + arrow blocks) to stack by hand, or floor boxes the child can walk.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Count the boxes from Bit to the star, then draw one arrow per box.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — box 1 to box 4 needs three right arrows.
3. Let them try. Children build a left-arrow stack (Ex 2) and a two-step stack (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Build 1: right, right, right (box 1 → 2 → 3 → 4, the star). Exercise 2 — Build 2: left, left (box 4 → 3 → 2, the star).
Exercise 3 — Build 3: right, right (box 1 → 2 → 3, the star).

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: too many or too few arrows. Count the boxes between Bit and the star first.
Make it easier: place a finger on each box and draw one arrow per box.
Make it harder: ask for a stack that starts somewhere else and still reaches the star.
Make it active: a child walks their built stack on the floor boxes to test it.

parts.title: Ontario Kindergarten link (official wording)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children plan and create a sequence of steps to reach a goal, then test and refine it.
In plain terms: writing your own stack of blocks to reach the star.
No reading is needed from the child — you read each prompt aloud; the child circles, numbers, or draws an arrow.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child builds a stack with the right arrows and number of steps to reach the star.
